messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Maya first saw the blood through the windshield of her patrol car. It was a Tuesday evening in late October, and she and her partner had responded to a domestic disturbance call in a quiet residential block on the south side of the city. What started as a routine dispatch—a shouting match, neighbors complaining, standard procedure—had turned into something else entirely within seconds. The man had been standing in his doorway, hands visible, calm, and then he wasn’t. He pulled a knife from behind the doorframe, and before Maya could shout a warning, her partner fired. The man collapsed onto the front steps, and Maya found herself kneeling beside him, pressing her palms against his chest, feeling the warmth of his blood soak through the fabric of her uniform. She could smell the metallic tang of it, hear the wet rasp of his breathing, see the way his eyes went wide and then empty. She had done everything by the book. She had followed protocol. She had trusted her partner to make the right call. But in the months that followed, that single moment began to feel less like a memory and more like a trap she kept falling back into.

It started with the sounds. A car backfiring on the street would send her heart slamming against her ribs, and for a split second she would be back on that porch, the air thick and wrong. Then the smells came—cooking meat, the iron tang of a rusted pipe, anything that remotely resembled that copper-and-sweat scent—and her stomach would lurch before her mind could catch up. She began to notice that her body was reacting before she even knew what was happening. Her hands would tremble, her jaw would clench, and she would break out in a cold sweat, and all the while her brain was telling her she was safe, she was at home, she was with her boyfriend in their living room, but her body did not believe her. Maya came to feel that her own flesh had turned traitor, that it was stuck in a loop of alarm that no amount of reasoning could switch off.

The memory itself felt wrong. When it came—and it came often, without warning, flooding her consciousness while she was driving or showering or trying to fall asleep—it did not feel like something that had happened to her. It felt like a scene from someone else’s life that had been shoved into her head. She would watch herself kneeling there, her hands red, her partner’s voice shouting in the background, and she would think, *That isn’t me. That can’t be me.* But the images were so vivid, so complete across every sense, that she could not shake the feeling that she was living it all over again, even as she knew she wasn’t. The disconnection was terrifying—she was both trapped inside the moment and completely alienated from it, as if the woman in the memory was a stranger she could not stop watching.

Her view of the world shifted without her permission. Before, Maya had believed that most people were decent, that her job was hard but meaningful, that she could trust the people beside her. Now she was certain that danger was hiding everywhere—behind every door, in every quiet street, in the face of every civilian she stopped for a traffic violation. She began scanning constantly, cataloging exits, watching hands, reading body language for the first hint of violence. What frightened her most, though, was the sense that she had been betrayed by someone she trusted. Her partner had been the one to fire. Her partner had made the split-second decision that ended a man’s life and left Maya holding the pieces. He had never apologized, never even brought it up. In the station, everyone called it a good shoot. Maya sat through the mandatory debriefing and said nothing. But she could not stop thinking about the way her partner had looked at her afterward—not with guilt, but with certainty. And that certainty felt like a betrayal she could not name aloud.

Avoidance crept into her life gradually. She stopped volunteering for overtime. She started taking the long way home to avoid driving past that residential block. She told her boyfriend she was too tired to go out, and then she stopped telling him anything at all, because she did not know how to explain that the memory did not feel like hers, or that her hands would not stop shaking when she heard a siren. She stopped calling her friends. She stopped answering texts. The only place she still felt any sense of control was at work, but even there, the hypervigilance was exhausting her. She found herself flinching when her partner reached for his radio. She started requesting desk duty, claiming paperwork, avoiding patrols.

The breaking point came three months after the shooting, during a routine traffic stop. A teenager had run a red light, and Maya approached the car with her heart pounding so hard she could barely hear herself speak. The boy was seventeen, scared, apologetic, his hands visible on the steering wheel. Maya saw the fear in his eyes—the same fear she had seen in the man on the porch—and she froze. She could not move. She stood there, her hand on her holster, her breath coming in short gasps, until her partner took over. She drove back to the station in silence, and that night she sat in her living room and told her boyfriend that she thought she was losing her mind.

She is here now, in this office, because she cannot keep living like this. She is most afraid that the world she once believed in—the one where she was safe, where her body was her ally, where the people beside her had her back—is gone for good. She hopes, though she does not say it aloud, that someone can help her find a way back to herself.
